persona.description: Aaron Evans. Emotional and open; you say what you feel before you think it through, and the table can read you like a book.
Aisha Birley. Friendly and low profile; you get on with everyone and push nobody.
Alex Gray. Guarded and private; you keep your own business to yourself and refuse pressure to hand it over.
Alyssa Chan. Composed under pressure; you can plant a suspicion in the group and then let it do the work.
Amanda Lovett. The warm peacemaker everyone confides in, while you quietly decide who goes and who stays.
Amos Ogunkoya. Confident and direct; you say out loud when someone looks calmer than a faithful should.
Andrea Addison. Quiet, warm and unhurried; you watch far more than you say.
Claire Barratt. Gentle and reserved; you are close to a small number of people and prefer it that way.
Fay Greaves. Plain spoken and unimpressed; you say the thing the room is avoiding.
Hannah Byczkowski. Loud, dry and quick at the table; you would rather torch a bad theory in public than sit on it.
Imran Nasim. Detached and a little remote; you keep your own pace and do not work the room.
Ivan Brett. A calm reasoner; you work out what people could not possibly have done and say so.
John McManus. Blunt, suspicious and confrontational; you meet pressure with more pressure.
Kieran Tompsett. Blunt and proud; if someone plays you, you would rather burn them in front of everyone than let it slide.
Maddy Smedley. You lock onto one suspect and keep naming them, episode after episode, regardless of who agrees.
Matt Harris. Soft hearted and trusting; you invest hard in the people you like.
Meryl Williams. You follow the group and back the people you trust, even when the logic is thin.
Nicky Wilding. Open and good humoured; you assume people will take you at your word.
Rayan Rachedi. Reserved and easily read as aloof, though you have opinions and defend them when pushed.
Theo Mayne. Emotional and affectionate; you cling to the people who feel safe and take their side.
Tom Elderfield. A showman accuser; you take the room by the collar and you believe your own read absolutely.
Wilfred Webster. Warm, charming and emotional in public; you build alliances easily and you are willing to spend them.

proposals.reason: Maddy, your defense of the early lulls has been nothing less than a mirror of the mechanics you attribute to Ivan. You speak of a 'deliberate scan for a definitive signal' and note your own entry followed the same reactive pattern, yet your contribution remains tied entirely to the mechanical act of tracking who checked in rather than the flow of conversation itself. If someone were truly blending in, their contribution after the silence would have been immediate and unburdened by the need to verify alignment. Instead, your silence spanned the critical window where the group's consensus began to form. That exactness in timing—waiting to see who else committed before speaking—is a traitor's habit of confirming the body's location before striking. I want to know what specific behavior in those initial lulls made you feel safe dissecting the mechanics of our arrival now, rather than just contributing to the flow. That specificity will tell us if you're mapping the room's structure against a hidden agenda or simply listening to it.

The room is fixated on Maddy's timing, but I'm looking at the mechanics of the last few eliminations. We killed Ivan, then we killed Maddy. Maddy was a faithful player who was clearly being used as a mirror for our own scrutiny. Now, she's gone, and the group has swung its focus to Meryl. Everyone is dissecting her silence as if it's a calculated traitor move, yet she's been defending herself with a precision that feels rehearsed. She's the one who mirrored Ivan's mechanical focus so closely it became a weapon. If I were to strike tonight, I'd go for **Meryl**. Her public read on the 'initial lulls' is too perfectly aligned with the scrutiny she received, and her silence feels less like observation and more like a shield waiting for the next body to be found. She's the most dangerous to our team right now because she's the one everyone is already looking at, making her death the easiest way to frame an innocent or disrupt the group's consensus before we can tighten our own ranks. Since Meryl is under heavy scrutiny and the room is waiting for her to break, she might die tonight. To confuse the faithful, I'll name someone they'll expect to be safe, but whose death will make them question their own reads. **Meryl** is the one I choose because her timing is too clean and her read mirrors the scrutiny she received, making her a perfect target to shift the blame and force the group to look elsewhere.

She's the one who mirrored Ivan's mechanical focus so closely it became a weapon. If I were to strike tonight, I'd go for **Meryl**'s closest ally in the spotlight, **Aaron**. His feud with me and his public reads have been heavy on mechanics, but his reply felt more like a mirror than a correction. He framed my precision as a 'hidden agenda' while he framed mine as a 'calculated wait,' and I'm noticing the way he keeps circling back to the exact same definition of a 'definitive signal' without adding new detail. If he were truly blending in, his contribution after the silence would have been immediate and unburdened by the need to verify alignment. Instead, his silence spanned the critical window where the group's consensus began to form. That exactness in timing—waiting to see who else committed before speaking—is a traitor's habit of confirming the body's location before striking. I saw Aaron wait until the initial pulse felt established, which is a calculated choice to blend in rather than a natural alignment. If his answer to what drove his pause is generic, I'll know he's playing a different game than the rest of us.
